# The HOA Board Will Now Come to Order

---

## I.

Fifty dollars a day.

The ramp had been up for eleven days, which meant the fine was five hundred and fifty dollars, which meant that by the end of the month it would be fifteen hundred, which meant that by the time Richard died — and Richard was dying, this was not speculation but the conclusion of two oncologists, a palliative care nurse, and the particular grey stillness that had settled into his face like weather — the ramp fine alone would exceed four thousand dollars, assuming sixty-two remaining days, which was the median, though Meredith knew better than most people alive that the median was not a promise. The median was a mannered lie that statistics told to comfort the innumerate. She was not innumerate. She had been a senior actuarial analyst for TransPacific Life & Casualty for twenty-three years. She held the FSA and the CERA. She had once built a mortality model for pipe fitters in the Gulf Coast region that was still in use eleven years later, and she could tell you, if you held still long enough to listen, the precise dollar value that a sixty-eight-year-old white male non-smoker with stage IV pancreatic cancer and supplemental Medicare represented to an insurance company, to a hospital system, to the federal actuarial tables, and now — as of eleven days ago — to the Creekview Estates Homeowners' Association, which had assessed the value of her husband's continued ability to leave and enter his own home at negative fifty dollars per twenty-four-hour period.

The ramp was pine. Her nephew Danny had built it over a Saturday and most of a Sunday, working from a YouTube video and a diagram he'd printed at the FedEx on Marsh Lane. It was not beautiful. It was functional. It had a gentle slope — one inch of rise per twelve inches of run, which Danny had measured with a level and a solemnity that made Meredith love him so fiercely she had to sit down on the porch step and pretend to check her phone. The ramp had no railing on the first day. Danny came back Wednesday and added one. It was pressure-treated lumber the color of weak tea, bolted to posts that Danny had sunk into the flowerbed where Meredith's knockout roses used to be. The roses were gone. She'd pulled them out herself. You could not have both roses and a ramp, and this was not a difficult calculation.

The violation notice had appeared on Tuesday, the day after the ramp went up, pinned beneath the brass door knocker with a paperclip that had left a small scratch on the finish. She had not noticed the scratch until the third time she read the notice, which was printed on Creekview Estates letterhead — a clip-art line drawing of a creek that did not exist near any of the estates — and signed by Douglas R. Whitmore, Board President, in a looping hand that conveyed, to Meredith's eye, a profound contentment with itself.

**NOTICE OF VIOLATION — §4.11(c): Exterior Modifications Requiring Prior Approval**

The relevant language was on page forty-one of the bylaws, a document Meredith now owned in three forms: the original PDF from the HOA website, a printed and spiral-bound copy she'd had made at the FedEx on Marsh Lane (Danny was there again, printing ramp diagrams for a neighbor; he looked at her spiral-bound bylaws and did not ask), and a highlighted edition in which she had marked every subsection, cross-reference, and internal contradiction in a color-coded system of her own devising. Yellow was definitional ambiguity. Green was procedural requirement. Pink was places where the document contradicted itself, which happened more often than you'd think, because the bylaws had been amended fourteen times in fifteen years, always by the same hand, always at annual meetings attended by no more than nineteen of the subdivision's eighty-six households, and always — Meredith had checked — without the thirty-day written notice required by Article XI, Section 2, "Amendment Procedures," which itself had been amended in 2016 without thirty days' written notice, a recursion that made Meredith want to laugh or set something on fire, and she was not a woman who did either.

Richard was asleep. Richard was often asleep now. The morphine made the world soft for him, which was good, because the world was no longer a place that rewarded his attention. He had been a shop teacher at Brennan Middle School for thirty-one years. He had all his fingers. He was proud of this. He would tell you about it, or he would have, before the talking became difficult and then optional and then rare. She could hear the oxygen concentrator from the dining room — a low mechanical hum that she had, in eleven days, learned to hear as silence, the way you stopped hearing a refrigerator. Except that she hadn't stopped hearing it. She heard it all the time. She heard it now, beneath the click of her actuarial calculator — the same Texas Instruments BA II Plus she'd carried since 1998, its buttons worn to a shine that looked, in certain light, like faith.

She sat at the dining table with the calculator, the three editions of the bylaws, and a yellow legal pad on which she had written, in her small square hand:

*Compounding variables:*
*— $50/day (§4.11(c), Schedule B, "Fine Assessment")*
*— No maximum specified*
*— No appeal timeline specified*
*— Architectural Review Committee = Doug, Doug's vote, Doug's proxy*
*— Annual meeting: 43 days*

Forty-three days. At fifty dollars a day, that was $2,150 in additional fines before she could even raise the issue in a forum where other human beings were present. She wrote this number on the legal pad. She looked at it. She drew a box around it. Then she turned to a clean page and began to write names.

---

Gloria Montez-Park arrived on a Wednesday evening carrying a stenotype machine in a leather case that was older than some of the people on Meredith's street. She set it on the dining table beside the legal pad and the calculator and the bylaws, and she flexed her fingers the way a pianist does, or a surgeon, or a woman who once transcribed eleven hundred pages of custody proceedings in the Family Court of Collin County and was removed from the certified shorthand reporters' registry for inserting parenthetical commentary into the record.

The commentary had been, in Gloria's view, restrained. When the father's attorney described his client's "unwavering commitment to the children's well-being," Gloria had typed *(Father was sixteen minutes late; coffee stain on shirt; children not present)*. When the mother broke down on the stand describing the night she found the apartment empty, Gloria had typed the testimony verbatim and then added *(witness is telling the truth)*. This was, the review board informed her, not her determination to make. She was a recorder. Her job was fidelity, not commentary. She could not editorialize. She could not interpret. She could not — and this was the word they used, the word that still made her jaw tighten six years later — *intrude.*

She had not worked as a stenographer since. But she still practiced. She transcribed talk shows, city council meetings, arguments at the post office. Her fingers needed to move the way some people's legs needed to run. And when Meredith called her — they knew each other from the book club, and before that from the elementary school auction committee, and before that from a neighborhood potluck in 2011 where they had stood in a kitchen together and said nothing to each other for nine minutes, which, in Meredith's view, was the foundation of all durable friendship — Gloria said yes before the question was finished.

Gloria's HOA violation was Section 4.11(c) — the same section as the ramp, the same section as everything, because 4.11(c) was the section that covered "any exterior modification visible from the street or from the common areas," which, in a subdivision where every house faced a street and every backyard abutted a common area, meant *everything*. Gloria had installed a satellite dish on her roof in 2019. It was small. It was for Korean television. Her mother-in-law had moved in after her husband's stroke, and the woman was eighty-one and spoke no English and wanted to watch her shows, and Gloria had called the cable company and learned that the Korean-language package was not available on their platform, and she had driven to a store on Royal Lane and bought a dish and paid a man named Terrence to install it, and she had not, in the velocity of her mother-in-law's grief and her own exhaustion, submitted an Architectural Review Request Form to the Creekview Estates HOA.

The fine was $50. Then $100. Then $200 — because, as Doug Whitmore explained at that year's annual meeting, in response to Gloria's written appeal, the fine schedule in the newly amended Section 4.11(c) included an escalation clause for "continuing violations not remediated within the initial thirty-day notice period." Gloria had remediated. She had removed the dish. Her mother-in-law sat in the living room and watched the local news in a language she did not understand, and when she asked, in Korean, where her shows had gone, Gloria said the cable was broken, and her mother-in-law nodded, because what else could she do. The fine was waived — eventually, after Gloria wrote a letter — but the dish was gone and the old woman never got her shows back and Gloria never forgot the particular way that Doug Whitmore had said "we appreciate your cooperation," which sounded, to Gloria's court-trained ear, *exactly* like a judge thanking a witness for testimony that had just been stricken from the record.

"I'll keep minutes," Gloria said, setting the stenotype on the table.

"We're not a board," Meredith said.

"Everything's a proceeding," Gloria said. "You just don't always know it yet."

---

Phil Carmendy arrived on Thursday, by foot, carrying a canvas tote bag from NPR that contained four books, a pocket-sized spiral notebook, a mechanical pencil, and a thermos of decaffeinated coffee so strong it had left a permanent brown ring on the inside of the thermos cap. The four books were all the same book: *Robert's Rules of Order Newly Revised*, in the 10th, 11th, and 12th editions, plus the pocket-sized *Robert's Rules of Order Newly Revised in Brief*, which Phil referred to as "the field manual" and which he kept in his left back pocket the way other men kept a wallet.

Phil had attended every meeting. Not every HOA meeting — every *meeting.* In the past eleven years, Phil Carmendy had attended the annual and quarterly meetings of the Creekview Estates HOA, the monthly meetings of the Collin County Water District, the biannual meetings of the Plano ISD School Board (he had no children), the weekly meetings of the Plano City Council, the quarterly meetings of the North Texas Municipal Water District, the annual meetings of two other HOAs in adjacent subdivisions (as a "concerned neighboring stakeholder," a designation he had invented and that no one had successfully challenged), and, on one occasion that he described with the hushed reverence of a man recalling a pilgrimage, a procedural workshop at the National Conference of State Legislatures in Denver, where he had asked a question during the Q&A that was later described by the moderator as "very thorough."

Phil's violation was Article VII, "Meeting Conduct and Decorum." Specifically, Article VII, Section 3: "Speakers during the open-comment period shall limit their remarks to three minutes and shall address only matters on the published agenda." Phil had exceeded his three minutes at the 2017 annual meeting by forty-seven seconds — he had timed himself afterward, reviewing the meeting from memory — while raising a point of order about the agenda itself, which he argued had not been distributed in compliance with the notice requirements of Article V, Section 1, which required fourteen calendar days' advance notice, whereas the agenda had been emailed thirteen days prior, on a Sunday, which Phil argued should not count because the HOA's own office hours, as listed on the website, did not include Sundays, raising the question of whether a communication sent outside of official operating hours constituted valid notice under the bylaws' own definitional framework.

Doug Whitmore had gaveled him silent.

Not gaveled — Doug didn't have a gavel. He had rapped his knuckles on the folding table at the front of the community room, twice, sharply, and said, "Phil, I think we've got the gist," and someone in the back had laughed, and the meeting had moved on, and Phil had sat back down with something rearranging itself inside his chest, something load-bearing shifting half an inch to the left, and in eleven years it had not shifted back.

"The problem," Phil said, standing in Meredith's dining room on Thursday evening, having declined a seat three times out of a conviction that important things should be said while upright, "the *problem* is that people think Robert's Rules is about bureaucracy. People think it's fussy. People think it's the boring part. But what Robert's Rules actually is — what Henry Martyn Robert understood when he wrote the first edition in 1876 after a disastrous church meeting in New Bedford, Massachusetts — is that *procedure is the only thing standing between the powerful and everyone else.* A rule is a wall. You don't notice the wall when you're inside the house. You notice it when someone's trying to throw you out."

Meredith looked at him. His thermos was under one arm. His NPR bag was over his shoulder. His eyes were the particular bright wet of a person who has been waiting a very long time to say something to someone who might actually listen.

"Sit down, Phil," she said.

He sat.

"How well do you know the Creekview bylaws?"

"I found eleven procedural deficiencies in the 2023 amendments alone."

Gloria's fingers moved over the stenotype, recording this.

"I found nine," Meredith said. She slid the pink-highlighted copy across the table.

Phil pulled his mechanical pencil from his shirt pocket. He opened the bylaws. Gloria transcribed the silence.

---

The book club arrived together on Saturday, because the book club always arrived together, not by arrangement but by a coordination so deeply embedded in seventeen years of shared practice that it had become autonomic, like breathing, or like the way all six of them could, without consulting one another, identify the precise moment in a novel when the author had stopped writing from lived experience and started writing from research. They had been meeting every third Thursday since 2007. They had read two hundred and nineteen books. They had been scheduled to discuss *Demon Copperhead* — which four of them had finished, one had abandoned at page 340, and one had listened to on audiobook at 1.5x speed during her commute and was prepared to defend this choice with the ferocity of someone who knew it could not be defended — but *Demon Copperhead* was not going to be discussed tonight, and all six of them knew it, because Meredith had sent a text to the group thread at 4:47 p.m. on Wednesday that read:

*I need help. Not book club help. Doug Whitmore help. My house Saturday at 6. Bring the highlighted bylaws if you still have yours.*

Four of the six still had theirs.

They were:

**Janet Okafor-Briggs**, retired high school principal, violation: Section 6.2(a), "Lawn Maintenance and Landscaping Standards." Janet had allowed her front lawn to include a three-foot patch of native prairie grass — little bluestem, inland sea oats, Mexican feathergrass — as part of a pollinator garden she'd planted with her grandchildren. The violation notice described it as "unkempt or neglected vegetation inconsistent with community standards." She had mowed it the next day. Her granddaughter, who was seven, had asked what happened to the butterflies' house. Janet had said the butterflies moved. She could not think about this without her hands shaking, so she didn't think about it, except on Wednesday when she got Meredith's text, and she thought about it, and her hands shook, and she picked up the highlighted bylaws from the shelf beside her bed and put them in her purse.

**Donna Kessler**, dental hygienist, violation: Section 5.3(b), "Holiday and Seasonal Displays." Donna had put up a twelve-foot inflatable Santa Claus the day after Thanksgiving 2021 — the same inflatable she'd put up every year since 2014, the same inflatable her late husband Marcus had bought at a Home Depot in Frisco the last Christmas before his diagnosis, the same inflatable her sons called Fat Santa and argued over who got to plug in, a ritual that had survived their father's death because rituals are the scar tissue of grief and you don't pick at scar tissue.
